name: Maltese Cross
description: Maltese Cross is a domino game played with a double-six set. It takes its name from the tableau layout that resembles a Maltese Cross. The game features a unique two-phase setup where players first build four arms around a central spinner, then add doubles crosswise to complete the cross shape before regular play continues.

history.origins: A member of the Cyprus family of domino games, named after the distinctive Maltese Cross pattern formed by the tableau during play.
timeline: Traditional: Played in Mediterranean regions with double-six domino sets
Modern: Remains popular as a family domino game
Present: Played worldwide as a classic domino variant
history.cultural: A social family game commonly played in Cyprus and Mediterranean regions.
history.evolution: The game can be adapted for larger domino sets (double-9, double-12) by adjusting the matching rules accordingly.

setup.deck: Standard double-six domino set (28 tiles). For 2 players: 7 tiles each. For 3-4 players: 5-6 tiles each.
setup.dealing: Tiles are dealt evenly. Remaining tiles form the boneyard.

rules.objective: Be the first player to play all your tiles (domino). Score the total pips remaining in opponents' hands.
rules.gameplay: The player with the highest double sets it as the spinner. Going clockwise, each player must play a tile matching the spinner until four tiles are around it (phase one). A player unable to play draws one tile from the boneyard; if it can play they set it, otherwise they keep it and pass. Once four arms are started, each player must add a double to the end of any arm (crosswise); all four arms must be completed (phase two). After that, doubles are played crosswise and non-doubles in line from the ends of the arms. Play continues until one player dominoes or the game blocks.
keyRules: Highest double starts as spinner in center
Phase one: four tiles around spinner, matching the spinner; draw from boneyard if unable to play
Phase two: add one double to end of each arm (crosswise); all four arms must be completed before free play
After phase two: doubles played crosswise, non-doubles in line from arm ends
First to play all tiles (domino) scores sum of pips in opponents' hands
If blocked, player with lowest total wins and scores (sum of others minus own); game to 60 points

strategy.basic: Try to hold two strong suits that total to seven (such as 2s and 5s). This gives you flexibility with the matador matching rule.
strategy.intermediate: The 0-0 (blank-blank) is the most valuable tile - it guarantees a play and can block one end of the train. Save matadors to change the end of the train when you don't have a matching tile.
strategy.advanced: If you have a double, try to set up an arm in phase one that will let you play it in phase two. For example, with the 6-6 double as spinner and you hold 5-6 and 5-5, play 5-6 on the spinner to guarantee playing 5-5 on the next turn.
tips: Leading with the highest double gives you control of setting the spinner
Force opponents to draw by making the train end on values they likely don't have
Save matadors for emergency plays when you're blocked

scoring.description: When one player dominoes, they score the total pips on tiles in opponents' hands. If the game blocks, the player with the lowest total wins and scores the sum of the others' pips minus their own. Game is played to 60 points (or more by agreement).
scoring.winCondition: First to play all tiles (domino) scores pips in opponents' hands; first to 60 points wins the game. If blocked, lowest total wins the round and scores (others minus own).
